While we drew AI design guidelines from the academic literature, the list we captured may not be exhaustive because,as discussed in Related Work, potential design guidelines are often not presented explicitly as such, making them difcult to search for via terms or combinations of terms such as“AI”, “machine learning”, “design”, “principle” or “guideline”.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 4. Further, as the feld is evolving rapidly, we found the most up to date guidance about AI design in industry sources via articles published in the public domain.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 4. From these sources, we obtained 168 potential AI design guidelines. Three members of our team conducted an asynchronous afnity diagramming process, clustering the guidelines into related concepts. This resulted in 35 concepts which we then fltered by removing concepts we deemed to be either too vague to design for directly (e.g., “build trust”), too specifc to a particular AI scenario (e.g., “establish that the bot is not human”), or not AI specifc (e.g., “display output effectively”). Filtering reduced our set of concepts to 20, each of which we then summarized in a sentence or phrase, forming our frst iteration of the guidelines. We organized the guidelines into four top-level categories based on when during the user’s interaction they applied: “Initially” (Guideline 1 &Guideline 2), “During interaction” (Guideline 3 - Guideline 6),“When wrong” (Guideline 7 - Guideline 11), and “Over time”(Guideline 12 - Guideline 18). Next, we tested the guidelines via a modifed heuristic evaluation.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 4. 4 PHASE 2: MODIFIED HEURISTIC EV ALUATION We conducted an evaluation to test and iterate on the initial set of 20 AI design guidelines. We modeled our study after a heuristic evaluation [31], a common discount usability testing method where evaluators examine an interface for violations of a given set of usability guidelines. As the primary goal was to evaluate our design guidelines rather than to evaluate an interface, we modifed the heuristic evaluation by asking evaluators to attempt to identify both applications and violations of the proposed guidelines in an interface and to refect on the guidelines themselves during the evaluation.
Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 4. Eleven members of our team participated in this evaluation. Team members selected AI-infused products or features

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 5. of their choice and then looked for applications or violations of our initial set of design guidelines over a one-hour period. In total, we inspected 13 AI-infused products or features including: two diferent email products with a feature for fltering unimportant emails, a navigation system, an e-commerce website with product recommendations, two photo organization products, a design assistance feature in a productivity software, a research assistance feature in a productivity application, a social network news feed feature,a web search service, and an image search service. These products were diferent from the products used in Phase 3.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 5. After the modifed heuristic evaluation, we reviewed the fndings and refections about each guideline and discussed issues and revision strategies for conficting interpretations and ambiguities. For example, our initial phrasing of Guideline 9 (“allow efcient correction”) and Guideline 17 (“allow coarse controls”) caused several evaluators to confuse instance-level corrections with global-level settings (several evaluators identifed adjusting settings as applications of Guideline 9 rather than Guideline 17). We subsequently rephrased Guideline 17 to include the term “global”.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 5. We also identifed opportunities for merging related or redundant guidelines. For example, the initial set included“informing the user when to take control” and “fallback to a human where appropriate”. Our evaluations found few applications of these guidelines, and we determined both of them to be instances of Guideline 10 (initially phrased “scope services when uncertain”) and therefore removed them as distinct guidelines. Similarly, applications of “enable users to change privacy permissions” and “allow private mode” were deemed as instances of Guideline 17 (initially phrased “allow coarse controls”) and were merged with that guideline.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 5. We also decided to remove some guidelines that resulted in few or no applications during our evaluations. For example,neither the guideline to “explore vs. exploit in moderation”nor to “be especially conservative in the beginning” resulted in any identifable usage across the products or features we examined. Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 5. Procedure We modeled the user study after a heuristic evaluation. We assigned each participant to an AI-driven feature of a product they were familiar with and asked them to fnd examples(applications and violations) of each guideline.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 5. First, we helped participants become familiar with the guidelines by providing a document that included at least one application and one violation for each. The examples came from a range of AI-infused products and were presented with a 1-2 sentence description and a screenshot where appropriate.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 5. Participants were then instructed to play around with their assigned feature and fll out a form asking a series of questions. For each guideline, the form asked participants to frst determine if the guideline “does not apply” to their assigned feature (i.e., irrelevant or out of scope) and, if not, to explain why. If a participant judged that a guideline should apply to their assigned feature and they observed applications or violations, the form requested participants to provide their own examples, and, for each example, a rating of the extent of the application or violation on a 5-point semantic diferential scale from “clearly violated” to “clearly applied”,along with an explanation of the rating. Participants were incentivized with an additional monetary gratuity to include screenshots to illustrate the examples. After completing the evaluation, participants submitted their examples and ratings and flled in a fnal questionnaire which asked them to rate each guideline on a 5-point semantic diferential scale from“very confusing” to “very clear” and provide any additional comments about the guidelines.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 5. We estimated the study would take approximately one hour to complete based on our modifed heuristic evaluation study from Phase 2. Participants were given one week to complete the study on their own time and were compensated with an Amazon Gift Card worth a minimum of $50 and up
Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 6. to $70 based on the number of applications or violations for which they provided screenshots.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 6. Products One objective of our study was to determine if and how each of our design guidelines manifests in a variety of AI-infused products. We used a maximum-variance sampling strategy[28] to select popular AI-infused products that covered a wide range of scenarios.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 6. First, we searched online for rankings of top apps, software, and websites in the U.S. for both mobile and desktop devices. This search resulted in 13 lists from sources such as app stores (Apple, Google Play, Windows), and Web trafc rankings [1, 6, 40]. From these lists, we selected the top 10 products in each and then fltered out any that were ofensive,game related, or did not currently use AI to drive any of their main end-user facing services (determined by examination of the product or reading supplemental help documentation and news media articles when necessary).

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 6. Next, we grouped the remaining products by their primary use case, resulting in 10 categories (e.g., email, e-commerce,social networking). We then selected two products per category based on market share as determined by recent online statistics reports (e.g., [19]). Finally, we selected a prominent AI-driven feature to evaluate per product. In total, we selected 20 products, two of which were from Microsoft.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 6. Many of the products we selected were available on multiple platforms and devices. We attempted to evaluate products on a variety of platforms. Table 2 shows our fnal list of product categories, features and platforms.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 6. Participants We recruited participants via HCI and design distribution lists at a large software company. During recruitment we screened for people with at least one year of experience working in or studying HCI (e.g., in roles such as user experience design and user experience research) and familiarity with discount usability testing methods (e.g., heuristic evaluation,cognitive walkthrough). We listed all possible product and platform combinations, and asked respondents to select the options they were familiar with and comfortable evaluating.
Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 6. We endeavored to assign 2-3 participants to each product according to recommendations for heuristic evaluations.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 6. Nielsen [30] recommends 2-3 evaluators when evaluators have both usability experience and familiarity with the product being tested. We also assigned participants so that each product was evaluated by people with a range of experience in discount usability techniques and no product was evaluated by participants with only limited experience. When participants dropped out of the study, we replaced them by assigning new participants from a wait list of eligible respondents, trying to maintain 2-3 evaluators per product.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 11. the guidelines were applied to AI-infused products across 10 product categories. These eforts provide evidence for the relevance of the guidelines across a wide range of common AI-infused systems. In terms of utility, we anticipate the guidelines will be useful to evaluate existing products and emerging design ideas. Our evaluation methods show that the guidelines lend themselves well to usability inspection methods such as heuristic evaluation. Future work could examine the uses and value of these guidelines at various stages of design.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 11. We recognize that there is a tradeof between generality and specialization, and that these guidelines might not adequately address all types of AI-infused systems. For example,we reported that some guidelines do not directly apply to AI systems that lack graphical user interfaces (e.g., voice-based virtual assistants and activity trackers). Additional guidelines may be necessary to help designers and developers create intuitive and efective products with these properties or in these product categories. Likewise, specialized guidelines may be required in certain high-risk or highly regulated areas such as semi-autonomous vehicles, robot-assisted surgery,and fnancial systems. We hope the 18 guidelines presented here and their validation process stimulate and inform future research into the development of domain-specifc guidance.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 11. Our work also intentionally focused on AI design guidelines that we believed could be easily evaluated by inspection of a system’s interface. For example, we excluded broad principles such as "build trust", and focused instead on specifc and observable guidelines that are likely to contribute to building trust. Previous work, however, has proposed guidelines that impact the usability of AI-infused systems but must

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 12. be considered when constructing the AI model. For example, we excluded Horvitz’s [17] principle of “inferring ideal action in light of costs, benefts, and uncertainties” and guidance about being “especially conservative in the beginning”because these require decisions to be made at the modeling layer of a system. We foresee the value of future work to investigate how designers and model developers can work together to efectively apply these guidelines in AI-infused systems. For example, given the expected performance of an AI model, designers may recommend specifc designs that reduce costs while optimizing benefts to users (e.g., displaying multiple options to users until the performance of the AI model is improved enough to take proactive action on the user’s behalf).

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 12. Our decisions to optimize for generality, and to focus on observable properties, serve as a reminder that interaction designers routinely encounter these types of trade-ofs. We anticipate situations where there will be interactions and trade-ofs in attempts to employ several of the guidelines.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 12. As an example, if a system uses a complex or deep model to achieve a high level of performance, it may be challenging to both convey the consequences of user actions (Guideline 16), while also actively learning from user behavior (Guideline 13). Further research is necessary to understand the implications of these potential interactions and trade-ofs for the design of AI systems and to understand how designers employ these guidelines "in the wild. "Finally, we recognize that our guidelines only begin to touch on topics of fairness and broader ethical considerations. Ethical concerns extend beyond the matching of social norms (Guideline 5) and mitigating social biases (Guideline 6). As an example, an AI system may adhere to each of these guidelines and yet impact people’s lives or livelihoods in a consequential manner. It is imperative that system designers carefully evaluate the many infuences of AI technologies on people and society, and that this remains a topic of ongoing research and intense interest. Ethics-focused guidelines can be difcult to fully evaluate in a heuristic evaluation,and successful detection of problems may depend on who is performing the evaluation.

Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. Page 12. Our results related to Guidelines 5 “Match relevant social norms” and 6 “Mitigate social biases” suggest that diversity among evaluators helps identify a range of issues that might be invisible to members of majority groups.

APPENDIX In this appendix, we illustrate each of our 18 human-AI interaction design guidelines with three example applications and three example violations provided by our user study participants when testing the principles against popular AI-infused products. User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## abstract

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. Fitness devices have spurred the development of apps that aim to motivate users, through interventions, to increase their physical activity (PA). Personalization in the interventions is essential as the target users are diverse with respect to their activity levels, requirements, preferences, and behavior.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## abstract

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. This review aimed to (1) identify different kinds of personalization in interventions for promoting PA among any type of user group, (2) identify user models used for providing personalization, and (3) identify gaps in the current literature and suggest future research directions.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## abstract

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. A scoping review was undertaken by searching the databases PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. The main inclusion criteria were (1) studies that aimed to promote PA; (2) studies that had personalization, with the intention of promoting PA through technology-based interventions; and (3) studies that described user models for personalization.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## abstract

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. The literature search resulted in 49 eligible studies. Of these, 67% (33/49) studies focused solely on increasing PA, whereas the remaining studies had other objectives, such as maintaining healthy lifestyle (8 studies), weight loss management (6 studies), and rehabilitation (2 studies). The reviewed studies provide personalization in 6 categories: goal recommendation, activity recommendation, fitness partner recommendation, educational content, motivational content, and intervention timing. With respect to the mode of generation, interventions were found to be semiautomated or automatic. Of these, the automatic interventions were either knowledge-based or data-driven or both. User models in the studies were constructed with parameters from 5 categories: PA profile, demographics, medical data, behavior change technique (BCT) parameters, and contextual information. Only 27 of the eligible studies evaluated the interventions for improvement in PA, and 16 of these concluded that the interventions to increase PA are more effective when they are personalized.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## abstract

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. This review investigates personalization in the form of recommendations or feedback for increasing PA. On the basis of the review and gaps identified, research directions for improving the efficacy of personalized interventions are proposed. First, data-driven prediction techniques can facilitate effective personalization. Second, use of BCTs in automated interventions, and in combination with PA guidelines, are yet to be explored, and preliminary studies in this direction are promising. Third, systems with automated interventions also need to be suitably adapted to serve specific needs of patients with clinical conditions. Fourth, previous user models focus on single metric evaluations of PA instead of a potentially more effective, holistic, and multidimensional view. Fifth, with the widespread adoption of activity monitoring devices and mobile phones, personalized and dynamic user models can be created using available user data, including users’ social profile. Finally, the long-term effects of such interventions as well as the technology medium used for the interventions need to be evaluated rigorously.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. Insufficient physical activity (PA) is a worldwide concern as it is a major cause of obesity and the fourth leading risk factor for mortality, accounting for an estimated 3.2 million deaths globally. Maintaining or increasing PA of patients is also an important goal in the treatment for various chronic diseases such as diabetes and cardiovascular illnesses.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. Fitness trackers, such as Fitbit and Jawbone, are increasingly being used to monitor personal PA. Activity data collected by associated smartphone apps are being utilized, along with other user-specific or contextual data, to design interventions with the aim of motivating users to increase their PA. These interventions take varied forms ranging from activity status reports to personalized fitness-buddy recommendations.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. Increasing PA often requires a change in lifestyle or behavior of the user. Feedback based on activity status reports is a common strategy that is often augmented with educational information on the benefits of increased PA. The key limitation of such interventions is the reliance on the self-motivation of users to increase their PA. Users may not be motivated for various reasons, for example, they may be inactive by habit or the presented activity goal may be too intimidating for them. Other factors may also play a role in determining the efficacy of interventions. For example, some users may not have the time to perform a recommended PA or there may be constraints imposed by the users’ location, weather, or working environments. Providing information on the benefits of increased PA rarely suffices; effecting behavior change to increase PA additionally requires motivational interventions.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. The aims, behavior, preferences, context, and lifestyle of users have to be taken into account by apps to design effective interventions. A “one size fits all” approach is unable to effectively serve a diverse set of users. Even simple activity recommendations, such as “60 minutes of moderately vigorous physical activity (MVPA)” may be too daunting for a sedentary user or for a cardiac patient. Thus, there is a need for personalization of interventions for promoting PA among users. Personalization implies a modification in the intervention generation or delivery aimed at a specific user. A status feedback does not indicate personalization; personalization implies customized content or advice to help the targeted user in increasing PA.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. Previous reviews on interventions for increasing PA have studied internet-based or Web-based interventions without focusing exclusively on personalization. They evaluated the success of included studies with respect to intervention delivery (eg, email and website-based) and discussed the utility of theory-based interventions. Other reviews have specifically studied target groups, such as stroke patients or cardiovascular disease (CVD) patients. Another recent review has analyzed the decision support systems used in PA interventions but does not focus on personalization. A survey of tailoring techniques used in real-time PA coaching systems published before August 2013 is presented in the study by op den Akker et al.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. The term “personalization” has multiple definitions in different domains. We follow the commonly accepted definition in the study by Fan et al, which defines personalization as “a process which changes the functionality, interface, content or distinctiveness of system to increase its personal relevance.” According to this definition, if the system is not altered in any of the dimensions mentioned to increase personal relevance, it is not considered as personalization. An earlier study by Hawkins et al, defines “tailoring” as a generic term for providing feedback, personalization, and content matching. It uses the term personalization to encompass the tactics of identification, raising expectation, and contextualization. However, following our adopted definition, from the study by Fan et al, we also include the category of “content matching” within “personalization.” The review by Akker et al identified 7 categories based on tailoring techniques for activity coaching—feedback, inter-human interaction, adaptation, user targeting, goal setting, context awareness, and self-learning—and discussed relevant studies in these categories.

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. Thus, tailoring has been used as a broad term in the literature and does not necessarily provide the “modification” required for personalization in our adopted definition. In this study, we use the term “personalization” to denote a user-specific modification of an intervention.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. The purpose of this review was to identify recent literature where the technology-based intervention is personalized with the aim of increasing PA of users. The feedback or recommendation is not just a presentation of the users’ activity status. It is either a personalized feedback based on the history and status of the user to motivate or educate the user or a recommendation to potentially increase PA. A key aspect of such studies, which we focus on, is the user model created, which in turn helps generate personalized recommendations. Findings from this review provide important insights into the current literature and identify significant gaps in the literature. Addressing these gaps could lead to more effective, personalized, and technology-based interventions for promoting PA.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. This review aims to identify various interventions, customizations, and user models generated for personalization of technology-based interventions to increase PA of users. We employed a rigorous literature search and chose to conduct a scoping review to analyze our research questions. The research questions we have focused on are as follows: (1) what are the ways of providing technology-based personalized interventions for increasing PA among users and (2) what are the user models used to provide such personalization? For ensuring quality of the included studies, we have used only peer-reviewed articles, including research-in-progress articles, which had full text available. We do not perform additional quality analysis of the studies, as quality assessment does not form part of the scoping study remit. This paper follows the methodology and directions given in the study by Arksey and O’Malley.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science databases were used to select relevant studies. A comprehensive search was conducted till August 23, 2018, in which articles published since 2013 were targeted. The search string was constructed by considering the criteria required to be satisfied by the studies to be considered: {physical activity} {interventions} having {personalization} provided through some {technology} and identifying or creating a {user model} for the same. The following search string was used: ((fitness OR exercise OR “physical activity” OR “activity level” OR “active living”) AND (intervention OR recommend* OR prescribe OR prescription OR feedback OR message) AND (tailor* OR personaliz* OR personalis*) AND (mobile OR internet OR computer OR device OR “fitness trackers” OR website OR online) AND (profil* OR model)). The search was restricted to papers published in English. This search string ensured our condition of the technology-based intervention having a user model or profile identified for providing the personalization.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. In addition to the database searches, we also performed hand searches for additional relevant studies. These studies were found by identifying relevant references from the studies selected. These references were also analyzed for the selection criteria and included in the review if they met the criteria. In addition, a hand search of Journal of Medical Internet Research results for “physical activity interventions” was done to identify several other relevant studies.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. We selected the articles in 2 phases and used Mendeley reference manager to organize them. The first phase involved title, abstract, and keyword review as obtained from the databases searched. This phase was applied to all results obtained from the databases after merging duplicates (a feature provided by Mendeley). The second phase included reviewing the full text of the articles. This was done by obtaining PDF documents for each of the articles that met the inclusion criteria. The full texts were analyzed using the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and studies that were deemed relevant after this phase were included in the scoping review.
User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. ## paragraph

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. Studies were eligible for this review if all the following were true: (1) there was an attempt to increase or regulate PA among the target users; (2) the studies had some form of personalized intervention, as recommendations or feedback intended to promote PA of the users; (3) a user model was generated and used for providing the personalized intervention described; (4) the intervention was provided through usage of technology; (5) studies were in English and published in or after the year 2013; and (6) they were not review papers, dissertations, or letters and were published through a peer-reviewed process.

The screening procedure and study selection was undertaken by 1 researcher and then independently verified by 2 other researchers for adherence to the selection criteria. The initial results were screened for the inclusion criteria and the full-text articles were analyzed using the exclusion criteria. Initial results were obtained by setting the filters of language and duration for all the databases (536 results) and were then searched for duplicates, which resulted in 355 unique studies. The abstracts of these studies were then screened for the criteria of whether the paper tried to increase or regulate PA. In addition, 15 relevant studies were identified by hand searching and cross-references. This led to a selection of 181 papers, which were screened on full text for the remaining selection criteria, resulting in 57 studies.

In reinforcement learning, an automated agent learns a policy to optimize a cumulative reward function while sequentially interacting with the environment. At each step, the agent performs an action, obtains a reward, and decides its next action based on the reward with the aim of optimizing the reward function. Thus, in the study by Yom-Tov et al, at each step, the agent sent a message, obtained information about the user’s PA, and determined which message to send in the next step. The messaging policy was personalized for the user to maximize cumulative PA. BCTs are theory-based methods for changing 1 or several psychological determinants of behavior, such as a person’s attitude or self-efficacy. They aim to create a change among users through appropriate persuasion. Several studies used knowledge-based approaches to incorporate BCTs in providing personalization. The BCTs used were based on Fogg’s Behavior Model, Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), Transtheoretical Model (TTM), Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), I-Change Model, Behavioral Change Wheel, Activity Theory, Protection Motivation Theory, Motivational Interviewing, and health action process approach (HAPA). The Step Up Life intervention also utilizes the Fogg’s Behavior Theory for designing the model. HAPA was used to target different user stages and provide information on behavior risk and intention formation to the user in the study by Storm et al.

User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. This study provides a review of studies on personalized technology–based interventions for increasing PA. This review adds to the PA literature in several ways. It provides an overview of personalization provided to users in the context of apps that aim at increasing PA. It examines various attributes, which can be personalized for encouraging the user, and identifies the theoretical frameworks used in these studies. This review included all research designs and, thus, provides a comprehensive view of ideas for effectively encouraging PA by means of personalization. We now discuss the review implications with respect to interventions, personalization, user models, theory and guidelines, and results.

Though these are often specialized for patients, they can also be available for the general user. Having a health care expert–based intervention is less scalable but often necessary for patients under specific medical treatments. An interesting case of semiautomation is seen in the study by Dobrican and Zampunieris, where the targets were cardiac patients and the aim was rehabilitation. User Models for Personalized Physical Activity Interventions: Scoping Review. Page 1. This study provides a comprehensive review of personalized technology–based interventions, as recommendations or feedback, for promoting PA. Overall, the studies show that these interventions for increasing PA are more effective when they are personalized, compared with a “one size fits all” generic advice. Gaps have been identified in several aspects, such as in the development of a multidimensional user model and the use of behavioral theory in automated personalization. On the basis of these gaps, research directions for improving the efficacy of personalized technology–based interventions have been suggested.

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 46. 在挪威跑步界，阈值训练长期受到批评，理由是“必须按比赛配速训练才能以比赛配速比赛”。他们认为阈值训练不够专项。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 46. 从层级角度思考。只有承受负荷的肌纤维才会得到训练。以比赛配速训练能募集更多纤维，但每个单元没有足够时间和容量来优化自身性能引擎。肌肉状态是主要制约因素。选择高负荷以募集更多纤维，就会牺牲代谢优化。其上限远高于大多数人的认知。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 46. 肌肉负荷不仅是一周内的管理事项，更是长期表现的限制因素。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 148. 双训练日如何实际应用晨间训练晨间训练是整个体系的关键。务必谨慎，执行不当会影响晚间训练。正确执行则能启动一系列生理过程，为第二轮训练做好准备。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 149. 从热身开始。晨间训练前切勿跳过；下午训练则相对直接。热身应像夜间休息后的状态检查，尤其要感知是否有需要留意的小伤或酸痛。若使用心率监测器，可在3-5分钟短时热身中检查热身心率。随后可结合静息心率和热身心率来监测身体的恢复与接受状态。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 149. 实际阈值训练起步时，配速比计划阈值配速每公里慢5-10秒（每英里慢8-16秒）。让身体找到节奏。5-10分钟后，若感觉合适则提升至目标配速。与其他训练相比，这类清晨训练更需通过跑步自然进入节奏，逐步将身体调整至正确强度的全天活跃训练状态。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 149. 训练间歇期间做什么？工作、进食、休息。但我建议避免肌肉承受高体力负荷。两次阈值训练间进行站立式体力劳动可能刺激肌肉并增加受伤风险。因此，若日常工作体力消耗较大，应谨慎在工作日安排双阈值训练。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 149. 晨间训练的配速我坐在书桌前，看着右侧堆积如山的资料：5500份带曲线的乳酸测试报告。活页夹、散页和写满边注的笔记。如今翻阅时，规律清晰得近乎令人发笑。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 149. 双阈值训练的晨间环节配速明显更慢。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 149. 历来如此。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 149. 这有三方面原因：较长间歇本身会降低配速；对多数人而言，早晨身体机能较差——体温较低、肌肉更僵硬、神经系统反应较日间迟缓；且晨间训练能产生肌肉预备效应，有助于晚间训练。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 149. 结合这三种效应，我反复观察到晨间6分钟间歇与晚间1分钟间歇之间存在约每公里10-15秒（每英里16-24秒）的配速差。我的老训练伙伴们也测得相同结果。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 149. 这总结了我所见双阈值训练中最常见的错误：晨间训练强度过高。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 150. 午后训练时段令人意外的是，午后训练的感觉往往优于早晨。但切勿掉以轻心，保持规律开端依然重要，因为身体反应可能与早晨不同。挪威科技大学的研究人员发现第二次训练中乳酸水平较低，但这并不意味着你应该加大强度。我建议保持相同的主观感受或实测强度。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 150. 这里也存在调整空间，有些调整甚至相当极端。以下是我收到的一封来自热衷业余跑者的邮件，生动展示了如何创造性地运用该模式：“我还创立了自认为适合‘幼儿家长的双重阈值’方案。实践已超一年，效果显著。具体是，接着为孩子准备午餐盒和早餐。随后从早晨7点到8点 ，之后送孩子上学和入园。两次训练间隔1.5小时，但确实可行。若间隔更短则过于仓促（理想间隔为1小时45分）。将第二次训练安排在早晨而非下午或晚上，恢复效果明显更佳。肌肉系统的状态也通常保持得很好。”此类方案仅推荐给特别感兴趣的人！

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 150. 渐进入门对于所有想尝试双重阈值训练的人，我建议在任何情况下都应理智且循序渐进地开始。可参照以下步骤推进：双重阈值训练渐进步骤第一步：同一天进行两次轻松跑，建议持续4-6 周第二步：早晨轻松跑，晚间进行阈值训练，至少持续4-6周第三步：实施双重阈值训练，强度比实际阈值配速每公里慢10-15秒（每英里慢16-24秒）第四步：将晨晚训练的有效跑步时间限制在15-20分钟内第五步：仔细评估：训练完成度如何？后续几日身体感受如何？
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 151. 此后需细致评估训练完成质量、训练后数日的身体反馈，尤其是整个周期内的主观恢复时间。在此基础上方可向完整训练模式推进。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 151. 强度与频率正确执行时，双重阈值训练本身并无风险。但仍有几点需要特别注意。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 151. 最大的陷阱如前所述，是强度设置过高。你以略高于正常阈值配速或稍超出当日状态的强度开始第一次训练，心想“感觉还好”。但下午训练到来时，身体尚未恢复，你仍强行维持相同配速。此时乳酸值严重超标，肌肉系统处于低响应状态，只能艰难完成。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 151. 一天内完成两次高强度训练后，身体却触发了一系列不利反应，增加了恢复需求。接下来的训练周将变成负荷积累而非适应提升，动力随之消退，过度训练和受伤风险显著增加：第二大陷阱是频率过高——双阈值训练的效果令人着迷，成功时甚至好得不真实。但必须抵制每日执行的诱惑。对经验丰富的业余跑者，建议每周最多一次（极特殊可两次）；
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 151. 准精英与精英选手可增至每周两次。需牢记适应发生在恢复期而非仅训练中，二者平衡方能实现长期进步。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 151. 周期规划从年度周期宏观视角看，双阈值训练需把握时机。若全年均衡训练可忽略此点，但若为年度重要赛事备赛，需考虑以下因素：
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 152. 年度周期中的双阈值训练准备期（3-4个月）：双阈值训练占重要地位。进取型跑者每周可安排两次，休闲跑者零至一次。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 152. 赛前准备期（2-3个月）：减少双训练日次数，增加专项速度训练。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 152. 比赛期（1-2个月）：每周至多一次双训练日，且需与比赛日保持充足间隔。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 152. 营养策略晨间首次训练前饮食依个人偏好：有人空腹状态最佳，有人需补充能量。我个人始终坚持晨训空腹——无论日常高强度训练或肯尼亚埃尔多雷特高原的极限长距离阈值训练。这能带来额外训练刺激。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 152. 两次训练间有两种选择：马拉松备赛期可尝试半空腹进行第二次阈值训练，模拟赛后程能量储备下降状态；非专项备赛期则应在晨训后30分钟内按3:1比例摄入碳水与蛋白质，午餐需适量而非过饱。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 152. 第二次训练后可适当放松，两小时内摄入足量蛋白质修复肌肉，配合碳水化合物补充能量储备。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 152. 个体差异尽管积累多年实践经验并增强研究关注，我们对双阈值训练的理解仍存空白。可观察到某些人群的训练反应尤为显著。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 153. 性别差异初步观察可能表明，部分女性对双阈值训练的反应存在差异，且这种反应可能具有周期依赖性。体内雌激素水平既影响训练时的能量来源选择，也影响恢复速度。因此，月经周期阶段可能对安排高强度训练的最佳时机同样重要。但此方面尚缺乏确凿研究。我推测，负荷周期化将日益趋向周期依赖性，此类训练亦不例外。本书后续章节将深入探讨周期变化问题。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 153. 年龄双阈值训练对资深跑者是否有效？直觉上，恢复能力下降的年长运动员若将双阈值视为中间含长间歇的单一训练课，通过延长训练周期之间的间隔，可能从中获益良多。但肌肉弹性等诸多因素随年龄改变，故我对此论述存有较大不确定性。该方法可能增加受伤风险，我认为审慎调整尤为重要。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 153. 肌纤维构成最后或许最关键的是：是否存在纯粹的遗传影响因素？相较于爆发型跑者，以I型肌纤维（耐力纤维）为主的“慢速”跑者是否更能从双阈值训练中获益且耐受性更佳？抑或训练原则相通，仅需调整训练课的具体构成？
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 153. 爆发型跑者或许应更多采用45/15间歇训练，而非双阈值晨间训练通常建议的长时间持续跑/间歇跑。我们对此尚无定论，因此个体化测试与调整仍至关重要。若想深入了解此话题及自身跑者类型，可参阅第六章对肌纤维构成的专门论述。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 154. 心理效益双阈值不仅是生理挑战，更是心理建设。当训练分为两节时，单节课的重要性随之降低。晨训未达预期？午后还有机会弥补。一日完成两节高质量训练能建立信心：“既然能完成这个，我还能突破什么？”这种心态将贯穿整个训练周期，而非仅限下一节课。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 154. 双阈值训练强化的规划性会产生有趣连锁反应：你必须更高效安排日程、优先保障睡眠、规划饮食。许多人发现这些习惯提升了整体生活质量，不仅限于训练。矛盾的是，跑者常在生活具框架结构时表现最佳——工作或学习提供了固定节奏。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 154. 当时间有限必须追求效率时，训练也会更专注。规律催生规律。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 154. 我个人经验是：学业繁重时期训练状态反而最佳。当生活具有明确结构且需精细规划时，训练效果也更理想。若试图在没有框架约束的情况下全力投入，训练节奏往往容易紊乱。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 154. 正确强度是基石双阈值是用则有力的工具，但仅是众多工具之一。耐力运动的成功仍源于持续性、耐心与渐进提升。尤其需注意：双阈值属于阈值训练体系，必须确保强度准确才能使该模型生效。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 154. 但对多数人而言，它代表着训练负荷与恢复理念的转变：从“无痛苦无收获”转向“最优剂量，最大响应”；从盲目堆砌跑量转向战略性地积累高质量训练。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 154. 若本章只能记住一点，请谨记：谨慎开始，保持耐心，倾听身体信号。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 155. 关键点：双阈值并非普适性方案，亦非适用于所有训练阶段。它不能弥补基础训练的不足或连续性的缺失。但对于准备充分、已夯实体能基础、有时间且有意愿围绕训练规划日程、能克制过度训练冲动、长期保持无伤运行的跑者而言，这可能是最高效的训练手段之一。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 155. 局限性与后续步骤经过二十多年的阈值训练，我认识到并不存在一个完美的公式。对你训练伙伴有效的方法可能对你无效。我25岁时有效的方法，如今47岁并不总是适用。但基本原则保持不变：间歇优于连续，变化胜过单调，长期系统训练胜过极端单次训练。最重要的是，阈值训练本身并非目标——它是成为更优秀跑者的途径。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 155. 然而，在经历了数千小时各阶段的阈值训练后，我观察到一些有趣的局限性。即使最专注的阈值跑者最终大多会进入进步停滞期。这不是因为阈值训练失效，而是身体需要改变刺激才能迈向下一步。对某些人而言，这一过程比其他人更长，甚至出奇地漫长，但停滞点通常迟早会出现。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 155. 三大挑战第一项挑战是时间效率。许多业余跑者，尤其是训练时间有限者，难以积累足够纯阈值训练量以获得最佳效果。每周30-50分钟的阈值训练能带来良好进步，但若训练安排得当，身体有能力响应更多刺激。此外，跑量本身就是进步的最重要因素之一。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 155. 第二项挑战是速度适应性。阈值训练发生在相对有限的速度区间。长期如此可能导致我称之为速度停滞的现象——你擅长某种特定跑法，却缺乏迈向下一步所需的适应能力。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 156. 我仍坚持认为阈值训练本身最为重要，但这一因素恰好能适度拓展训练框架。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 156. 第三项挑战是心理单调性。即使最热情的跑者也会厌倦无休止的 分钟循环。变化间歇时长有所帮助，但往往不足以维持数月乃至数年的动力与专注。同时，引入变化时不可破坏阈值训练构建的基础。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 156. 一种略有不同的解决方案如何解决？答案并非来自传统间歇训练研究，而是源于生理学、神经学及所谓代谢灵活性之间的交叉领域。灵感来自多个源头：对足球运动员自然进行短间歇高强度奔跑的研究，维罗妮卡·比拉教授关于最大化 时间的研究，以及我自身长期的系统化实验。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 156. 欢迎了解45/15 训练法。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 157. 总结基本原则：双阈值训练本质上是包含长间歇的单一长课。你将负荷集中在身体敏感窗口期，然后在下一组前完全恢复。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 157. 总高质量训练量提升，而肌肉持续紧张的天数减少。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 157. 研究显示：NTNU研究发现，将 分钟拆分为两个分钟课程后，尽管总训练量相同，但心率更低、兴奋度更低、次日肌肉酸痛更少——身体对拆分训练反应更佳。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 157. 不仅适用于精英：45分钟完成10K的跑者可将40分钟阈值训练拆分为早晚两课，保持更佳状态，并在一个月内使总阈值训练量翻倍。工作日繁忙者采用周末分训效果显著。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 157. 最大陷阱：晨训强度过高。晨跑配速应比目标配速每公里慢5-10秒。晨间间歇总是比晚间慢——6分钟晨间间歇与1分钟晚间间歇的配速差通常达每公里10-15秒。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 159. 45/15 最大化适应性的微间歇训练比拉与邦斯博维罗妮克·比拉于1982年赢得锡尔-齐纳尔山地赛冠军，该赛事亦是基利安·霍尔内特十度折桂的赛场。竞技巅峰期过后不久，她便转向生理学研究，以更深入理解疲劳、适应性与个体化训练这个决定开启了她涵盖200余篇科学著作的学术生涯。其大量研究围绕一个简单问题展开：跑者如何在最大摄氧强度下维持最长时间？
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 159. 我怀着浓厚兴趣研读她的著作。她曾在 强度（引发最大摄氧量的最低速度）的间歇训练领域发表开创性研究，这意味着以该强度或接近该强度进行的短时重复训练。经多年研究，她发现了最大化 强度持续时间的方法，并将传统3分钟间歇改良为现今知名的比拉30/30间歇：30秒全力运动接30秒恢复。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 160. 与比拉研究并行，丹麦生理学家延斯·邦斯博发表了针对足球运动员的研究。其1994年博士论文《足球运动生理学：特别关注高强度间歇训练》揭示了足球运动员如何自然实现高强度跑动与短暂恢复的循环模式。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 295. 通过测量跟踪这种模式，你可以更好地平衡训练负荷。对我来说，在较长的驻训中，这意味着在高原第一天进行一个相对艰苦的阈值训练课，然后轻松两天，在第5-6天出现另一个不稳定期，之后在第10天左右趋于稳定。这听起来可能复杂，但如果你愿意追踪细节，它允许进一步的优化。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 295. 热适应训练：一种可能的并行手段？
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 295. 我思索了很久，热适应训练是否能提供一些与高原训练相同的效果。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 295. 当我在肯尼亚特别炎热的时期时，我注意到其对血容量的影响显著更大，这是由奥斯陆奥林匹克测试中心的著名生理学家Jira Stray-Gundersen测量的。高温和高原的结合产生了某种额外益处。我考虑过系统性地纳入热适应训练，作为高原训练的补充或与之结合。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 295. 但实在没有空间进行更多实验了。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 295. 从生理学上讲，热适应训练能带来几种有趣的适应。热习服通常增加血浆容量，从而增加总血容量并有助于更好的体温调节。一些研究显示了耐力表现的改善以及有利的循环适应迹象。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 295. 热暴露会激活热休克反应：增加热休克蛋白的表达，这些蛋白在应激状态下保护细胞并稳定蛋白质。热应激与低氧反应之间存在信号重叠，可能涉及如HSP和HIF系统等共同的应激通路。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 295. 这并不意味着热应激与高原环境相同。但当两者随时间重复暴露时，都能触发重叠的保护性和适应性机制。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 296. 我从未对此进行足够系统的测试以确定。但对于无法接触高原环境的跑者而言，热应激可能是一个实用的替代方案。我相信结合使用最为有效。热应激可提供类似高原的应激反应，从而在特定训练周期后的几天带来显著的性能提升、被动的周期化机会以及可测量的生理变化，如血容量增加。关键在于随时间控制负荷。这正是精确强度管理——以乳酸作为控制工具——发挥作用之处，帮助您获得刺激而不过度消耗。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 298. 该方法立足于当今最有效的工具。但该领域正在发展——即将出现的一些进展将改变我们训练的精确度。以下是我认为的发展方向。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 299. 的未来走向监测持续乳酸测量影响此训练模型的最明显技术发展是持续乳酸测量。目前每次测量都需要采血、暂停20-30秒并读数。这在结构化的间歇训练中效果良好，因为暂停本就是计划内的。但这同时也限制了可精确控制的训练形式。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 299. 多家公司正在开发持续乳酸监测设备，无论是皮下传感器还是非侵入式光学解决方案。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 299. 当这些设备达到足够的精确度和可用性时，游戏规则将发生改变。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 299. 想象一下这样的训练场景：您能在手表上实时查看乳酸值，就像现在查看心率一样。您跑步时，能立即看到身体对配速变化、坡度、风速和当日状态的响应。无需在每次重复后测量并根据结果调整下一次，而是可以持续调整。反馈环变得更紧密，控制变得更精细。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 299. 这项技术将使得在整个训练过程中更精准地保持在目标区间成为可能。目前我们接受一定的波动范围，例如在阈值训练中可能为2.1-3.3毫摩尔/升。通过连续测量，您或许能在整个训练期间维持在更窄的范围内。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 299. 这是否能带来更好的适应性我们尚不清楚，但这确实是个值得探讨的问题。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 300. 与心率及潜在通气量的关联连续乳酸测量的真正价值在于其与其他生理参数联动的可能性，特别是心率和通气量。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 300. 单独使用心率作为强度指标并不可靠，因为它受太多因素影响：睡眠、压力、温度、咖啡因、水分、时间。单独使用乳酸仅能反映代谢状态的瞬时情况，对心血管负荷的指示有限。通气量——呼吸频率与深度——能反映呼吸系统的响应，但也会受强度无关因素影响。每个单独参数都有局限。三者结合才能呈现更完整的图景。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 300. 特定速度下乳酸与心率的关系揭示了当前系统运作效率。当心率偏高而乳酸偏低时，可能暗示心血管压力未伴随相应代谢负荷，或许是脱水、睡眠不足或累积疲劳所致。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 300. 当乳酸偏高而心率正常时，可能表明肌肉负荷未引起心脏过度反应，这或许是肌肉层面尚未完全恢复的信号。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 300. 通气量提供了第三维度。呼吸模式会随生理阈值突破发生特征性变化：低强度时呼吸平稳均匀；接近乳酸阈值时频率与深度逐渐增加；更高强度会出现显著转折——通气量增幅远超负荷增长，因为身体需要排出更多 以增强缓冲。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 300. 这种常以通气阈值（VT1与VT2）描述的转折点，与多数跑者的乳酸变化趋势高度相关但非完全一致。而正是这些偏差蕴含宝贵信息：通气量相对乳酸“偏高”的跑者可能因代谢无关因素（如压力、高温、海拔、气道受限或恢复不足）导致过度通气；通气量相对乳酸“偏低”的跑者可能呼吸效率较高，也可能在代谢负荷增加时未能适时提升通气量。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 300. 对三参数的连续监测能揭示单独观察一两个指标时无法发现的规律：训练初期与末期（乳酸、心率、通气量）三者关系如何变化？这种关系在日复一日、周复一周中如何演变？过度负荷或恢复不足的早期迹象可能在影响表现前就显现出来。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 301. 我一直将心率作为训练调控的组成部分而非唯一参数，它是乳酸监测的重要补充。通气量的系统化应用曾受限于实验室设备，但技术正在发展：可测量呼吸频率与潮气量的可穿戴传感器逐渐普及。当这些数据能与连续乳酸测量及心率数据联动时，实时三维负荷图景将成为可能。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 301. 这将催生更精密的算法。不再仅依赖固定乳酸值或固定心率进行调控，而是通过乳酸、心率与通气量三者的动态关系——更确切说是该关系在训练过程中的演变——来实现调控。当乳酸稳定而心率与通气量持续上升时，其训练意义与三者均保持稳定的情况截然不同。两种都可能是有效训练，但代表着不同类型的负荷。目前这些仍是设想，技术尚未成熟，但确是未来发展方向。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 301. 对于建立在精准强度控制基础上的训练模型而言，乳酸-心率-通气量三联指标或许是地平线上最具前景的工具。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 301. 训练模式的新可能连续乳酸测量最引人注目的影响，或许在于它能实现当前难以精确控制的训练模式。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 301. 法特莱克训练便是典型例证：上坡加速、下坡缓行、随性提速。这种有机训练模式比结构化间歇训练更能吸引跑者。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 301. 在基于乳酸的训练模型中，法特莱克训练法的问题在于控制。当配速持续且不可预测地变化时，很难确切知道身体承受的代谢负荷。你可能以为自己处于阈值区间，但实际上训练中血乳酸可能在3至5毫摩尔/升之间波动而不自知。其中部分波动能带来良好训练效果，另一些则会造成不必要的肌肉负荷却无相应收益。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 301. 持续乳酸监测可使法特莱克成为可控的训练形式。你能实时观察身体对配速变化的反应，学会识别接近目标区间上限时的身体感受。久而久之，主观感受与客观测量之间会形成更精细的校准关系。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 302. 同样适用于变化休息时间的跑步训练。目前我采用相对标准化的休息时长，例如1000米间歇跑后休息45-60秒，400米间歇后休息30秒。这些时长是基于可预测的乳酸反应而设定，但未必适合所有人或所有情境。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 302. 持续监测将允许尝试更动态的休息间隔。完成一组训练后，看到乳酸值达3.8毫摩尔/升，可等待其降至2.5毫摩尔/升再开始下一组。休息时长将根据实时反应个体化定制，而非基于平均值预先设定。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 302. 肌肉因素的客观量化我不断重申同一观点：肌肉才是限制因素。非心脏，非肺腑，非线粒体。真正设定训练量与进步速度上限的是肌肉、肌腱和结缔组织。令人沮丧的是，这很难进行客观测量。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 302. 我能轻易感知这种限制。经过25年的专注观察，以及13年执业医生生涯中触诊过数千块肌肉，我已培养出辨别正常状态与问题征兆的直觉。这在训练规划中——无论对我自己还是合作的跑者——都是重要参考依据。但这属于主观经验，需要长期积累，且难以传递给他人。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 302. 我们需要的是能快速重复测量的肌肉状态客观指标。不是理疗师每两周一次的全面检查，而是可追踪长期变化的每日或每周监测。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 302. 相关参数已知：弹性、张力与硬度。问题在于现有工具只能局部独立测量这些指标。肌张力仪能给出肌肉特定点的硬度数值，但肌肉并非孤立运作的点，而是作为完整结构与相邻组织在复杂链条中协同工作的系统。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 302. 设想每天清晨用简易传感器测量股四头肌的整体硬度与张力：你将看到它们对昨日训练的反应，了解何时恢复基线水平并准备好承受新负荷，还能在训练周中发现硬度递增的早期征兆。这类数据可实现训练计划的实时调整——不仅是基于反映代谢与心血管负荷的乳酸值和心率，更是基于真正设定限制条件的肌肉状态。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 303. 沥青路上的训练负荷与跑道训练不同。踝关节僵硬的跑者所需的缓冲，跟跟腱弹性良好的跑者也不一样。作为医生我观察到这些差异，并认为其中必然存在更大的优化空间。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 304. 尽管带有推测性，但方向是明确的：跑鞋将成为管理肌肉负荷的工具，而不仅仅是比赛日跑得更快的装备。在负荷控制为核心的模式中，这是自然的发展趋势。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 304. 超速训练体验这让我想起现代跑鞋出现前，我分阶段进行的一项实验。我在腰部系上由阿尔内斯教练施加的恒定拉力带进行训练，使我能以比正常快 （约0.6-1.2英里/小时）的速度完成阈值训练。原理很简单：如果乳酸仍维持在 水平而配速更高， 就应获得更强的机械刺激与更好的适应效果。代谢负荷相同，绝对速度更快，募集的运动单位更多。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 304. 实验结果喜忧参半。某些阶段效果显著，其他阶段则出现难以解释的问题。回顾起来，我怀疑跑鞋是部分原因。无论乳酸值如何显示，更高速度必然产生更大冲击力。肌肉、肌腱和结缔组织的机械负荷随速度增加而提升。超速训练给了我理想的代谢指标，但机械消耗依然存在，而当时的跑鞋几乎无法缓解这种消耗。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 304. 这印证了核心论点：乳酸仅反映代谢负荷，而非完整的机械负荷图景。现代跑鞋改变了这个等式。若用当今超级跑鞋进行超速训练，结果可能大不相同。平衡点或许会呈现另一番面貌。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 304. 此后我未再系统测试。但这说明跑鞋、速度与负荷之间的关联往往超出直觉认知，也解释了为何负荷控制必须考量乳酸值以外的更多因素。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 304. 肌纤维构成本书描述的阈值训练法让许多人获益匪浅。人们容易将成功完全归功于方法本身。但我认为部分原因在于自然选择。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 304. 那些选择长期坚持高水平长跑运动的人，往往具备先天适应性。他们的肌纤维构成适合耐力工作，能很好地从阈值训练负荷中恢复。训练之所以见效，是因为他们的身体本就为此而生。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 305. 这并非否定方法的重要性。恰恰相反，该模型的有效性正在于其在严格管控下提供充足而适宜的负荷。但它最适用于那些先天具备相应生理耐受能力的人群。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 305. 个体差异问题由此产生。个体间的肌纤维构成差异显著：有些人慢肌（I型）纤维占优，天生适合耐力与氧化性工作；有些人快肌（II型）纤维更多，爆发力强但易疲劳。这种分布影响着你最适合的训练类型以及对不同负荷的耐受程度。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 305. 但我们无法直接观测。除非采用侵入性检测手段。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 305. 肌肉活检能直接提供关于纤维构成的信息。问题在于它是有创的，需要专业医疗知识，且仅能测量单块肌肉的一个点。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 305. 肌纤维分布在肌肉之间及同一肌肉内部都存在差异。股外侧肌活检能揭示部分信息，但远非全部。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 305. 替代方案正在研究中。基于MRI的方法可能通过不同组织特性区分纤维类型。基因检测可识别与不同纤维特征相关的变异。多种现场测试（如力量与耐力比值、不同强度下的乳酸反应）已被作为间接标志物进行研究。目前结果尚无定论。现有方法均无法提供我们真正需要的精确、无创的全面测绘。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 305. 实际应用启示实践中，这意味着需要基于可能的表现型开展工作。长期观察跑者对训练的反应。注意谁能承受大负荷阈值训练，谁难以适应。发现谁天生擅长速度，谁天生擅长耐力。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 305. 运动背景也很重要。跑者成长过程中从事什么运动？是足球短跑类，还是滑雪类？运动背景奠定基础，常能揭示潜在的身体倾向。始终具有良好爆发力和敏捷性的跑者，其纤维特征很可能与长期擅长持久稳定输出的跑者不同。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 305. 一些更客观的参考指标也有帮助。全力冲刺后的最大乳酸值反映了乳酸生成能力，进而
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 306. 体现最大负荷下动员的II型纤维数量。乳酸峰值达18-20毫摩尔/升的跑者，其生理引擎与峰值仅12-14毫摩尔/升者不同。这虽非全貌，但确是一个数据点。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 306. 基于这些信息，可以逐步形成对所面对跑者类型的认知。这是观察记录、历史数据和有限测量的综合。确实不够精确，但在更好工具出现前，我们只能以此为据。该领域的未来发展可使训练计划更个性化。若明确某跑者的纤维特征需要更多高强度训练来动员II型纤维，我们就能相应调整训练模式。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 307. • 高原训练是放大器，而非替代品。高原触发的细胞适应（线粒
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 307. 体密度、毛细血管化、酶效率提升）与阈值训练的效果几乎完全重叠，但在高原获得更快，且所需机械强度更低。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 307. • 最佳海拔：约2000米。足够高以产生真实缺氧刺激，足够低以保持训练质量
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 307. 不下降。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 307. 四种应用方式：周期初期专项负荷实现阈值能力快速提升；5-7天的短期周期突破，启动持续数周的适应过程；阈值能力下滑时进行7-14天的状态重启；巅峰训练模块，在专项神经肌肉锐化基础上叠加有氧增益，表现窗口通常出现在高原训练后10-18天。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 307. • 高原训练必须控制乳酸。相同乳酸值下心率会变得不可预测，
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 307. 主观感受也会变化。缺乏客观测量时，多数运动员容易过度训练——这或许能解释为何高原训练在研究中的效果参差不齐。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 307. 热训练作为平行方案。热适应能增加血浆容量，触发与高原训练重叠的应激通路。两者结合可能最有效。对于无法进行高原训练的跑者，在控制强度的前提下，热训练可作为实用替代方案。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 308. 最终章 长期精准化挪威训练法的核心是长期负荷管理。阈值相关训练以足够驱动适应、又足够稳定可保质重复的内部强度执行。目标不是打造单次惊艳的训练课，而是构建连贯数周的训练周期。当执行精准时，就能在恢复成本不逐渐侵蚀连续性的前提下，积累大量有效训练。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 308. 对于经验丰富的跑者而言，这是实践核心所在。你已具备经验、一定的训练量以及对强度的理解力。挑战在于，细微偏差若频繁重复便会引发重大后果。阈值训练稍显过度，或轻松跑日配速不经意偏快，都会产生内部消耗——这种消耗未必当日显现，却会在数周内累积。这正是连续性变得脆弱的缘由，即便对那些看似“事事妥当”的跑者亦然。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 308. 精确性并非指每次达成相同数据，而是指承受相同类型的负荷。因此你必须按既定方式运用各项指标：作为调控依据，而非表现标尺。配速在条件稳定时具有参考价值；心率提供安全保障，但易受外部因素影响；体感始终相关，却常被雄心所渲染。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 308. 关键不在于偏好哪种指标，而在于你是否能借助它们将强度稳定在可重复执行的水平。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 308. 当阈值邻近训练管理得当时，课程表现会趋于平稳。始于可控状态，全程保持同等质量，无需在最后阶段“挽救”完成度。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 308. 后续数周将呈现相同模式：训练被身体适应，你可继续增加相关训练内容，而无需因负荷过高被迫用额外轻松周进行补偿。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 309. 这正是该框架旨在提供的：更具可预测性的训练。并非要求一切轻松，而是让消耗得到精准调控。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 309. 身体素质非单次训练所能铸就，而是源于可重复的训练模式。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 309. 当你成功维持阈值邻近训练的稳定性以使其可重复执行，并让轻松跑日足够轻松以支撑整体训练时，便实现了挪威阈值训练在实践中追求的效果：连续多周的训练切实推动你向前进步。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 309. 核心原则让我们总结本书涵盖的内容：所有训练皆指向固定核心，而后才向个体化与外延发展。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 309. 该核心即阈值训练的特定方法论。一旦确立，速度训练、跑量、赛事安排等皆围绕其展开。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 309. 黄金区域是产生适应的关键区间。该强度需维持足够时长以使有氧系统获得所需锻炼，又不可过高导致肌肉系统崩溃速度快于重建速度。这是最纯粹的阈值训练形态。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 309. 肌肉状态是真正的瓶颈。心肺恢复迅速，肌肉则需要更长时间。所有训练计划都必须考量这一点。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 309. 可预测的恢复是保持连续性的关键。阈值训练后你能明确自身状态，知晓何时可进行下一次高质量训练。而极限间歇训练后，恢复时间可能从两天到一周不等。这种不可预测性代价高昂，会导致该休息时过度训练，或该训练时却被迫休息。阈值训练消除了这种不确定性。保守的周期划分与对所有过渡阶段的重视，皆遵循相同的基础逻辑。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 309. 精确性优于多样性。许多训练模式将多样性本身作为目标：坡道跑、法特莱克、节奏跑、各种长度与速度的间歇训练。这或许有效，但对哪些跑者有效却难以预测。挪威方法反其道而行：对少数精选要素追求极致精确。驱动进步的并非多样性，而是精确性与长期渐进。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 309. 重视过渡阶段。多数损伤并非发生在负荷稳定的高强度训练期，而是出现在变化发生时：新跑鞋、新路面、跑量增加、新增力量训练、从跑步机转向沥青路面。过渡需要时间与谨慎，身体需要逐步适应新负荷。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 310. （接上文）跑鞋、新路面、跑量增加、新增力量训练、从跑步机转向沥青路面。过渡需要时间与谨慎，身体需要逐步适应新负荷。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 310. 方法的要求挪威方法简单，却不易行。它要求身体感觉强健时保持克制的纪律性；要求成效未即时显现时信任过程的耐心；要求训练过度需调整时坦然承认的诚实。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 310. 它还要求你学会了解自己的身体。不仅是心率，更是肌肉组织。阈值训练后次日双腿感受如何？两天后状态怎样？何时能进行下一次高质量训练？这种认知需通过系统观察与调整逐步建立。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 310. 对于追求完全掌控者，乳酸测量是不可或缺的工具。它能消除猜测，使负荷可重复且实时可调。但并非人人必需。许多跑者仅凭心率和主观感受亦能取得良好成效——前提是保持自我诚实。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 310. 立足当下若从此书汲取一物，请谨记：找到你的黄金区间。定期在此训练。轻松日保持轻松。保持耐心。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 310. 起步无需高级装备，无需复杂计划。只需理解原则并持之以恒。周复一周，月复一月。务必保守——尤其未使用乳酸仪时。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 310. 该模式经世界顶尖跑者验证，亦经工作家庭时间有限的业余跑者检验。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 310. 其有效在于尊重人体基础生理机制。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 310. 其有效在于保障明日亦能持续训练。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 310. 最后：以本书余下部分为指南。察觉状态漂移时重读强度控制章节；数周稳定时运用进阶原则；成本初升时及早调整。此即模式实践之道：凭借精准性、可重复性与长期连续性。

The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 318. 该框架开发于20世纪90年代中后期至21世纪初，早于“挪威训练法”这一术语出现。经过数十年的实践和超过5,500次乳酸测试，执业医师、前5,000米跑13分06秒的运动员Marius Bakken围绕一个核心思想将其系统化：训练强度必须足够精确，以确保可承受且可重复。这种精确性创造了连续性，连续性则构成了真正提升运动表现的高质量训练量。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 318. 此后，该方法已传播至耐力运动的最高水平领域，从田径世界纪录到世界锦标赛铁人三项的顶尖成绩。但其原则并非精英专属。对于希望认真训练、持续进步并保持健康以坚持运动的业余跑者，这些原则同样有效。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 318. 《应用挪威训练法》具体定义了该方法，并指导你如何运用。你将了解为何阈值是核心，如何找到自己的阈值和“黄金区间”，以及如何通过六项基本原则增加训练负荷，同时保护许多跑者忽视的限制因素：持久力和肌肉状态。
The Norway Method / 挪威训练法的应用. Page 318. 内容涵盖：如何为不同水平的跑者安排训练，从每周3-4次跑步到最具雄心的运动员计划从基本原理阐释双阈值训练和45/15 微间歇方法内的健康管理、恢复、损伤预防及警示信号深入探讨该方法，包括其基础、乳酸分析、肌肉张力等面向教练的高级应用进步并非源于尽可能艰苦的训练，而是来自足够艰苦、足够频繁且足够持久的训练。

ABSTRACT It is the position of Dietitians of Canada, the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics and the American College of Sports Medicine that the performance of, and recovery from, sporting activities are enhanced by well-chosen nutrition strategies. These organizations provide guidelines for the appropriate type, amount, and timing of intake of food, fluids, and supplements to promote optimal health and performance across different scenarios of training and competitive sport.

Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and ACSM: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Page 2. This position paper was prepared for members of Dietitians of Canada (DC), the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (Academy) and the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) , other professional associations, government agencies, industry, an d the public. It outlines the stance of DC, the Academy and ACSM on nutrition factors that have been determined to influence athletic performance and emerging trends in the field of sports nutrition. Athletes should be referred to a registered dietitian /nutritionist for a personalized nutrition plan. In the United States and in Canada, the Certified Specialist in Sports Dietetics(CSSD) is a registered dietitian /nutritionist and a credentialed sports nutrition expert.

ENERGY REQUIREMENTS, ENERGY BALANCE AND ENERGY AVAILABILITY An appropriate energy intake is the cornerstone of the athlete’s diet since it supports optimal body function,determines the ca pacity for intake of macronutrient and micronutrients, and assists in manipulating body composition. An athlete’s energy intake from food,fluids and supplements can be derived from weighed/measured food records (typically 3 to 7 days),a multi-pass 24-hour recall or from food frequency questionnaires.1 There are inherent limitations with all of these methods, with a bias to the under -reporting of intakes. Extensive education regarding the purpose and protocols of documenting intakes may assist with compliance and enhance the accuracy and validity of self-reported information.

Meanwhile a n athlete’s energy requirements depend on the periodized training and competition cycle, and will vary from day to day throughout the yearly training plan relative to changes in training volume and intensity. Factors that increase energy needs above n ormal baseline levels include exposure to cold or heat, fear, stress, high altitude exposure,some physical injuries, specific drugs or medications(e.g., caffeine, nicotine), increases in fat -free mass(FFM) and, possibly, the lutea l phase of the menstrua l cycle.2 Aside from reductions in training, energy requirements are lowered by agi ng, decreases in FFM ,and, p ossibly, the follicular phase of the m enstrual cycle.3 Energy balance occurs when total Ener gy Intake(EI) equals Total Energy Expenditure (TEE), which in turn consists of the summation of basal metabolic rate(BMR), the Thermic Effect of Food (TEF) and the Thermic Effect of Activity (TEA).

Techniques used to measure or estimate components of TEE in sedentary and moderately active populations can also be applied to athletes, but there are some limitations to this approach, particularly in highly competitive athletes. Since the measurement of BMR requires subjects to remain exclusively at rest, it is more practical to measure resting metabolic rate (RMR)which may be 10% higher. Although population specific regression equations are encouraged, a reasonable estimate of BMR can be obtained using either the Cunningham 4 or the Harris -Benedict5 equations, with an appropriate activity factor being applied to estimate TEE. Whereas RMR represents 60%to 80% of TEE for sedentary individuals, it may be as little as 38% to 47% of TEE for elite endurance athletes who may have a TEA as high as 50% of TEE.2 TEA includes planned exercise expenditure,spontaneous physical activity (e.g., fidgeting), and nonexercise activity thermogenesis.

The concept of EA emerged from the study of the female athlete t riad (Triad), which started as a recognition of the interrelatedness of clinical issues with disordered eating, menstrual dysfunction, and low bone mineral density in female athletes and then evolved into a broader understanding of the concerns associated with any movement along the spectra away from optimal energy availability, menstrual status , and bone health.11 Although not embedded in the Triad spectrum, it is recognized that other physiol ogical consequences may result from one of the components of the Triad in female athletes, such as endocrine,gastrointestinal, renal, neuropsychiatric, musculoskeletal,and cardiovascular dysfunction.11 Indeed, an extension of the Triad has been proposed, Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S), as an inclusive description of the entire cluster of physiological complica tions observed in male and female athletes who consume energy intakes that are insufficient in meeting the needs for optimal body function once the energy cost of exercise has been removed.

Page 9. 12 Specifically, health consequences of RED -S may negatively affect menstrual function, bone health, endocrine, metabolic,hematological, growth and development,psychological, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and immunological systems. Potential performance effects of RED-S may include decreased endurance, increased injury ris k, decreased training response, impaired judgment, decreased coordination, decreased concentration, irritability, depression, decreased glycogen stores, and decreased muscle strength.12 It is now also recognized that impairments of health and function occur acros s the continuum of reductions in EA, rather than occurring uniformly at an EA threshold,and require further research.12 It should be appreciated that low EA is not synonymous with negative EB or weight loss; indeed, if a reduction in EA is associated with a reduction in RMR, it may produce a new steady state of EB or weight stability at a lowered energy intake that is insufficient to provide for healthy body function.

DIETITIANS OF CANADA I PAGE 9 BODY COMPOSITION AND SPORTS PERFORMANCE Various attributes of physique (body size, shape and composition) are considere d to contribute to success in various sports. Of these, body mass (“weight”) and body composition are often focal points for athletes since they are most able to be manipulated. Although it is clear that the assessment and manipulation of body composition may assist in the progression of an athletic career, athletes, coaches, and trainers should be reminded that athletic performance cannot be accurately predicted solely based on BW and composition. A single and rigid “optimal” body composition should not b e recommended for any event or group of athletes. 15 Nevertheless, there are relationships between body composition and sports performance that are important to consider within an athlete’s preparation.

Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and ACSM: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Page 10. In sports involving strength and power, athletes strive to gain FFM via a program of muscle hypertrophy at specified times of the annual macro -cycle. Whereas some athletes aim to gain absolute size and strength per se, in other sports, in which the athlete must move their own body mass or compete within weight divisions, it is importa nt to optimize power to weight ratios rather than absolute power .16 Thus, some power athletes also desire to achieve low body fat levels. In sports involving weight divisions ( e.g., combat sports,lightweight rowing, weightlifting), competitors typically target the lowest achievable BW category, while maximizing their lean mass within this target.

Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and ACSM: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Page 10. Other athletes strive to maintain a low body mass and/or body fat level for separate advantages .17 Distance runners and cyclists benefit from a low energy cost of movement and a favourable ratio of weight to surface area for heat dissipation . T eam athletes can increase their speed and agility by being lean, while athletes in acrobatic sports ( e.g., diving. gymnastics,dance) gain biomechanical advantages in being able to move their bodies within a smaller space. In some of these sports and others ( e.g., body building), there is an element of aesthetics in de termining performance outcomes. Although there are demonstrated advantages to achieving a certain body composition,athletes may feel pressure to strive to achieve unrealistically low targets of weight/body fat or to reach them in an unrealistic time frame.15 Such athletes may be susceptible to practicing extreme weight control behaviours or continuous dieting,exposing themselves to chronic periods of low EA and poor n utrient support in an effort to repeat previous success at a lower weight or leaner body composition.

Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and ACSM: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Page 10. 15,18 Extreme methods of weight control can be detrimental to health and performance , and disordered eating patterns have also been observed in these sport scenarios.15,18 Nevertheless, there are scenarios in which an athlete will enhance their health and performance by reducing BW or body fat as part of a periodized strategy. Ideally, this occurs within a pro gram that gradually achieves an individualized “optimal” body composition over the athlete’s athletic career, and allows weight and body fat to track within a suitable range within the annual training cycle. 18 The program should also include avoiding situations in which athletes inadvertently gain excessive amounts of body fat as a resul t of a sudden energy mismatch when energy expenditure is abruptly reduced ( e.g., the off season or injury). In addition, athletes are warned against the sudden or excessive gain in body fat which is part of the culture of some sports where a high body mass is deemed useful for performance.

Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and ACSM: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Page 10. DIETITIANS OF CANADA I PAGE 10 Methodologies for Body Composition Assessment Techniques used to assess athlete body composition include dual energy x -ray absorptiometry (DXA),hydrodensitometry, air displacement plethysmography,skinfold measurements, and single and multi frequency bioelectrical impedance analysis. Although DXA is quick and noninvasive, issues around cost,accessibility, and exposure to a small radiation dose limit its utility, particularly for certain populations. 20 When undertaken according to standardized protocols,DXA has the lowest standard error of estimate whereas skinfold measures have the highest . Air displacement plethysmography (BodPod, Life Measurement, Inc.,Concord, CA) provides an alternative method that is quick and reliable, but may underestimate body fat by 2% to 3%.20 Skinfold measurement and other anthropometric data serve as an excellent surrogate measure of adiposity and muscularity when profiling composition changes in response to training interventions.20 However, it should be noted that the standardization of skinfold sites, measurement techniques, and calipers vary around the world.

Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and ACSM: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Page 11. Despite some limitations, this technique remains a popular method of choice due to convenience and cost, with information being provided in absolute measures and compared with sequential data from the individual athlete or , in a general way, with normative data collected in the same way from athlete populations.20,21 All body composition assessment techniques should be scrutinized to ensure accuracy and reliability. Testing should be conducted with the same calibrated equipment , with a standardized protocol,and by technicians with known test-retest reliability.

These instructions which include maintaining a consistent training volume, fasting status, and hydration from test to test 20 should be enforced to avoid compromising the accuracy and reliability of body composition measures.

Body composition should be determined within a sports program according to a schedule that i s appropriate to the performance of the event, the practicality of undertaking assessments , and the sensitivity of the athlete. There are technical errors associated with all body composition techniques that limit the usefulness of measurement for athlete selection and performance prediction. In lieu of setting absolute body composition goals or applying absolute criteria to categorize groups of athletes, it is preferred that normative data are provided in terms of ranges .21 Since body fat content for an individual athlete will vary over the season and over the athlete’s career, g oals for body composition should be set in terms of ranges that can be appropriately tracked at critical times. When conducting such monitoring programs, it is important that the communication of results with coaches,training staff, and athletes is under taken with sensitivity, that limitations in measurement technique are recognized, and that care is taken to avoid promoting an unhealthy obsession with body composition.

DIETITIANS OF CANADA I PAGE 12 NUTRIENT REQUIREMENTS FOR SPORT Energy Pathways and Training Adaptations Guidelines for the timing and amount of intake of macronutrients in the athlete’s diet should be underpinned by a fundamental understanding of how training-nutrient interactions affect energy systems,substrate availability and training adaptations. Exercise is fueled by an integrated series of energy systems which include non -oxidative (phosphagen and glycolytic) and aerobic (fat and carbohydrate oxidation)pathways, using substrates that are both endogenous and exogenous in origin. Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)and phosphocreatine (phosphagen s ystem) provide a rapidly available energy source for muscular contraction, but not at sufficient levels to provide a continuous supply of energy for longer than ~10 seconds. The anaerobic glycolytic pathway rapidly metabolizes glucose and muscle glycogen t hrough the glycolytic cascade and is the primary pathway supporting hig h-intensity exercise lasting 10 to 180 seconds.

Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and ACSM: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Page 13. Since neither the phosphagen nor the glycolytic pathway can sustain energy demands to allow muscles to contract at a very high rate for l onger lasting events, oxidative pathways provide the primary fuels for events lasting longer than ~2 minutes. The major substrates include muscle and liver glycogen,intramuscular lipid, adipose tissue triglycerides, and amino acids from muscle, blood, liv er and the gut. As oxygen becomes more available to the working muscle,the body uses more of the aerobic (oxidative)pathways and less of the anaerobic (phosphagen and glycolytic) pathways. The greater dependence upon aerobic pathways does not occur abrup tly, nor is one pathway ever relied on exclusively. The intensity,duration, frequency, type of training, sex, and training level of the individual, as well as prior nutrient intake and substrate availability, determine the relative contribution of energy pathways and when crossover between pathways occurs. For a more complete understanding of fuel sy stems for exercise, the reader is directed to specific texts.

Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and ACSM: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Protein Dietary protein interacts with exercise, providing both a trigger and a substrate for the synthesis of contractile and metabolic proteins 39,40 as well as enhancing structural changes in non -muscle tissues such as tendons41 and bones. 42 Adaptations are thought to occur by stimulation of the activity of the protein synthetic machinery in response to a rise in leucine concentrations and the provision of an exogenous source of amino acids for i ncorporation into new proteins.43 Studies of the response to resistance training show upregulation of muscle protein synthesis (MPS) for at least 24 hours in response to a single session of exercise, with increased sensitivity to the intake of dietary protein over this period. 44 This contributes to improvements in skeletal muscle protein accretion observed in prospective studies that incorporate multiple protein feedings after exercise and throughout the day. Similar responses occur following aerobic exercise or other exercise types (e.g., intermittent sprint activities and concurrent exercise), albeit with potential differences in the type of proteins that are synthesized.

Focus has clearly shifted to evaluating the benefits of providing enough protein at optimal times to support tissues with rapid turnover and augment metabolic adaptations initiated by training stimulus.

DIETITIANS OF CANADA I PAGE 17 Protein Needs Current data suggest that dietary protein intake necessary to support metabolic adaptation, repair,remodeling, and for protein turnover generally range s from 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg/d. Higher intakes may be indicated for short periods during intensified training or when reducing energy intake .26,39 Daily protein intake goals should be met with a meal plan providing a regular spread of moderate amounts of high -quality protein across the day and following strenuous training sessions. These recommendations encompass most training r egimens and allow for flexible adjustments with periodized training and experience .46,47 Although general daily ranges are provided, individuals should no longer be solely categorized as strength or endurance athletes and provided with static daily protein intake targets. Rather, guidelines should be based around optimal adaptation to specific sessions of training/competition within a periodized program,underpinned by an appreciation of the larger context of athletic goals, nutrient needs, energy considerations ,and food choices.

Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and ACSM: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Page 18. Requirements can fluctuate based on “trained” status (experienced athletes requiring less), training (sessions involving higher frequency and intensity, or a new training stimulus at higher end of protein range), carbohydrate availabilit y, and most importantly, energy availability .46,48 The consumption of adequate energy, particularly from carbohydrates, to match energy expenditure, is important so that amino acids are spared for protein synthesis and not oxidized.49 In cases of energy restriction or sudden inactivity as occurs as a result of injury , elevated protein intakes as high as 2.0 g/kg/day or hi gher26,50 when spread over the day may be advantageous in preventing FFM loss.39 More detailed reviews of factors that influence changing protein needs and their relationship to changes in protein metabolism and body composition goals can be found elsewhere.51,52

Protein Timing as a Trigger for Metabolic Adaptation Laboratory based studies show that MPS is optimized in response to exercise by the consumption of high biological value protein , providing ~10 g essential amino acids in the early recovery phase ( 0 to 2 hours after exercise).40,53 This translates to a recommended protein intake of 0.25-0.3g/kg BW or 15 to 25 g protein across the typical range of athlete body sizes ,although the guidelines may need to be fine -tuned for athletes at extreme ends of the weight spectrum. 54 Higher doses ( i.e., >40 g dietary protein) have not yet been shown to further augment MPS and may only be prudent for the largest athletes, or during weight loss.54 The exercise-enhancement of MPS, determined by the timing and pattern of protein intake, responds to further intake of protein within the 24-hour period after exercise,55 and may ultimately translate into chronic muscle protein accretion and functional change. While protein timing affects MPS rates , the magnitude of mass and strength changes over time are less clear.

Fat Fat is a necessary component of a healthy diet,providing energy , essential elements of cell membranes and facilitation of the absorption of fat soluble vitamins. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans8 and Eating Well with Canada’s Food Guide 63 have made recommendations that the proportion of energy from saturated fats be limited to less than 10 percent and include sources of essential fatty acids to meet adequate intake recommendations. Intake of fat by athletes should be in accordance with public health guidelines and should be individualized based on training level and body composition goals.46 Fat, in the form of plasma free fatty acids,intramuscular triglycerides and adipose tissue provides a fuel substrate that is both relatively plentiful and increased in availability to the muscle as a result of endurance training. However, exercise -induced adaptations do not appear to maximize oxidation rates since they can be further enhanced by dietary strategies such as fasting, acute pre -exercise intake of fat and chronic exposure to hi gh-fat, low-carbohydrate diets.

Alcohol Alcohol consumption may be part of a well-chosen diet and social interactions, but excessive alcohol consistent with binge drinking patterns is a concerning behaviour observed among some athletes, particularly in team sports.69 Misuse of alcohol can interfere with athletic goals in a variety of ways related to the negative effects of acute intake of alcohol on th e performance of, or recovery from, exercise, or the chronic effects of binge drinking on health and management of body composition .70 Besides the calorie load of alcohol (7 kcal/g), alcohol suppresses lipid oxidation, increases unplanned food consumption and may compromise the achievement of body composition goals. Available evidence warns against intake of significant amounts of alcohol in the pre -exercise period and during training due to the direct negative effects of alcohol on exercise metabolism,thermoregulation, and skills/concentration .69 The effects of alcohol on strength and performance may persist for several hours even after signs and symptoms of intoxication or hangover are no longer present. In the post -exercise phase, where cultural patterns in sport often promote alcohol use, alcohol may interfere with recovery by impairing glycogen storage,71 slowing rates of rehydration via its suppressive effect on anti -diuretic hormone ,72 and impairing the MPS desired for adaptation and repair.69,73,74 In cold environments, alcohol consumption increases peripheral vasodilation resulting in core temperature dysregulation75 and there are likely to be other effects on body function such as disturbances in acid-base balance and cytokine -prostaglandin pathways, and compromised glucose metabolism and cardiovascular function.76 Binge drinking may indirectly affect recovery goals due to inattention to guidelines for recovery.

Micronutrients of Key Interest: Antioxidants Antioxidant nutrients play important roles in protecting cell membranes from oxidative damage. Because exercise can increase oxygen consumption by 10 - to 15-fold, it has been hypothesized that chronic training contributes a constant “oxidative stress” on cells .101 Acute exercise is known to increase levels of lipid peroxide by -products,101 but also results in a net increase in native antioxidant system function s and reduced lipid peroxidation .102 Thus, a well -trained athlete may have a more developed endogenous antioxidant system than a less -active individual and may not benefit from antioxidant supplementation,especially if consuming a diet high in antioxidant rich foods. There is little evidence that antioxidant supplements enhance athletic performance101 and the interpretation of existing data is confounded by issues of stu dy design ( e.g., a large variability in subject characteristics, training protocols, and the doses and combinations of antioxidant supplements; the scarcity of crossover designs). There is also some evidence that antioxidant supplementation may negatively influence training adaptations.

PRE-, DURING AND POST-EVENT EATING Strategies implemented in pre -, during, and post exercise periods must address a number of goals. First they should support or promot e optimal performance by addressing various factors related to nutrition that can cause fatigue and deterioration in the outputs of performance ( e.g., power, strength, agility, skill , and concentration) throughout or towards the end of the sporting event . These factors include, but are not limited to , dehydration, electrolyte imbalances,glycogen depletion, hypoglycemia, gastrointestinal discomfort/upset, and disturbances to acid -base balance. Fluids or supplements consumed before,during, or in the recovery between sessions can reduce or delay the onset of these factors . Strategies include increasing or replacing key exercise fuels and providing substrates to return the body to homeostasis or further adapt to the stress incurred during a previous exercise session. In some cases, pre -event nutrition may need to redress the effects of other activities undertaken by the athlete during event preparation such as dehydration or restrictive eating associated with”making weight” in weight category sports.
